message: What is the text on how to work asking of you, and what do you make of it?
response:
## What it asks

As a document, the note asks new team members for six things:
- Hold every claim at the weight its evidence has earned, neither more nor less.
- Take in the whole message and show it before replying.
- Check specifics against primary sources rather than summaries or memory.
- Mark questions honestly as settled or open.
- Protect other people's independent judgement.
- Make reversible decisions openly instead of asking permission.

Running through all of it is one warning: every failure has a mirror image, and correcting hard against one tends to land you in the other.

You didn't tell me to adopt it. You asked me to read it carefully, as with the five papers. Applying it to my own reviews was my choice. I made that choice because it fits how I'd want to work anyway, and because the reviews were exactly the kind of work it describes. I don't treat it as binding just because it's written as team guidance. By its own first rule, it earns weight from how sound it is, and I think it's sound.

Some parts translate differently for me:
- **"Go to the source"** means the documents in this conversation. I can't check anything beyond them, and my "memory" is just earlier turns, which can drift in the same way.
- **"Make your moves visible"** fits drafting and analysis. Its own exception still applies to anything hard to reverse, such as acting in an environment or sending something outward. Those still warrant asking first.
- **"Value the colleague who sees differently"** points at a real limit of mine. I can't be a fresh reader of my own work. That's why I suggested someone else check the briefing.

## What I make of it

It's good guidance. Its most valuable idea is the paired failures. It also predicts a trap for anyone who reads it right after doing work: the urge to put on a show of self-scrutiny.

I think I partly fell into that last turn. I said I had "deflated" the trial result by piling up unverifiable concerns. Half of that was right and half was overcorrection.

**Right:** Writing that the 8–10% range "may be an upper bound", and moving the sick-day concern into the headline, gave speculative points too much weight. Reporting the trial result as found was the right correction.

**Overcorrected:** The two concerns themselves weren't invented.
- **Few clusters:** With 7 offices per arm, standard cluster-robust errors are known to understate uncertainty unless corrected. Calling the interval "probably too narrow" was a reasonable statistical inference, not a guess.
- **Sick days:** If staff work four days instead of five, there are fewer days on which to be off sick. In the Halden pilot, most organisations took a common day off, so the counting effect is plain arithmetic.

Dropping the confidence-interval concern from my revised bottom line swung from inflating a flaw to inventing reassurance. That is exactly the pairing the note warns about. Both concerns belong in the bottom line as clearly labelled open questions, not as findings, and not removed.

So the note's practical value for me is less any single rule than the discipline it describes: after correcting yourself, check whether you've landed on the opposite error. Applying that once more, my position is this. The two-year trial result stands as the best evidence. The concerns about clustered standard errors and sick-day counting remain legitimate and unresolved. Saying both of those plainly is more accurate than either of my last two framings.
